per_question.question: Who is eligible for the Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)? What requirements does someone have to meet to get in?
per_question.agent_answer:
To be eligible for CAP/DA, a person must be an NC Medicaid beneficiary and must need a nursing-facility level of care, but be able to receive needed care safely and cost-effectively in the community with CAP services rather than in an institution. [Policy 3K-2 § 2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Main eligibility requirements

A person must be enrolled in NC Medicaid, and their Medicaid eligibility category can still limit whether this particular service is available to them. [Policy 3K-2 § 2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

CAP/DA is for Medicaid beneficiaries who require institutional care, but whose care can be provided safely and cost-effectively in the community with CAP services. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

More specifically, Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary meets all of these criteria: [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

- The person meets the required HCBS nursing-facility level of care as determined by NC Medicaid and needs long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, directly related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- A completed CAP assessment shows a reasonable indication that the person will need at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within 30 calendar days of the evaluation. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person has a signed service plan authorizing one or more waiver services to be provided monthly, in a way that helps prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Or, for certain short-term situations, the person has a signed service plan authorizing equipment, modification, or technology needed to return to or remain in the primary private residence and prevent institutional placement, with installation completed within three calendar months of service plan approval. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person can maintain health, safety, and well-being in their primary private residence or another approved location with formal and informal supports. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person’s paid care needs can be maintained within the average institutional cost of the CAP/DA waiver. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person has a primary physician who can link and coordinate all medical services. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- The person has an emergency back-up and disaster plan identifying who will provide care when key staff or a primary caregiver cannot do so, including during public health emergencies. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## What “nursing-facility level of care” [unverified quote — not found in retrieved sources] means here

The policy says the HCBS level-of-care standard is aimed at applicants and active beneficiaries who meet a nursing-facility level of care because of a medical diagnosis or physical disability. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

That determination is based on conditions, diagnoses, and treatments showing care needs that meet or exceed Medicaid State Plan nursing-facility criteria, plus deficits in activities of daily living that show a need for the supplemental and supportive services the waiver can provide. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

A level-of-care determination must be completed at initial enrollment, is re-determined annually, and a change in condition that means the person no longer meets HCBS level of care can lead to disenrollment. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Other participation requirements

Covered services under this policy must be medically necessary, individualized, safe to furnish, and not primarily for convenience. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The emergency and disaster plan is a mandatory requirement that must be completed during service-plan development or within 30 calendar days of the initial or annual service-plan approval, and it must be updated quarterly or during an emergency or pandemic. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

If the person wants consumer-directed services, they must also complete a mandatory self-assessment and introductory training, understand the rights and responsibilities of directing their own care, and be willing and emotionally capable to act as an employer or choose a representative who can do that. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

They also must have an approved service plan identifying the amount, duration, frequency, and NPI of CAP/DA and non-CAP/DA services, receive services in compliance with applicable laws and policy requirements, and sign the Beneficiary Rights and Responsibilities. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Waitlist / priority status

CAP/DA participation is considered on a first-come, first-served basis, but some people are moved to the top of an existing waitlist if they meet listed priority criteria. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Priority groups include people ages 18-20 transitioning from CAP/C, people transitioning from a nursing facility in certain circumstances, certain APS-protected adults at risk, people with Alzheimer’s disease or related disorders, and adults already in another approved 1915(c) HCBS waiver who want to transition to CAP/DA if eligibility requirements are met. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:_s325
Title: Community Alternatives Program (CAP)
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched medicaid.
Content:
A Medicaid CAP Waiver authorized under § 1915(c) of the Social Security Act and Medicaid funds; to provide home and community-based services to Medicaid beneficiaries who require institutional care, but for whom care can be provided cost effectively and safely in the community with CAP services. CAP beneficiaries must meet all Medicaid eligibility requirements. CAP Programs consist of the following:
Community Alternatives Program for Children: CAP/C
Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults: CAP/DA
Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults choosing consumer-directed services: CAP/CD

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:3.4.8
Title: 3.4.8 CAP/DA In-Home Aide Service I
Section: 3.4.8
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched provider.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover a service for a beneficiary that, during the hours-of-service provision, provides limited to greater assistance with or monitoring of a minimum of two Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). The CAP/DA beneficiary must be unable to perform these tasks independently due to a medical condition identified and documented on a validated assessment. The need for assistance with or monitoring of ADLs relates directly to the beneficiary's physical, social, environmental and functional condition. In-Home Aide Services, when listed in the service plan, are provided in the community, home, workplace, or educational settings.
The provider(s) subject to the EVV requirements that provide In-Home respite shall comply with Section 12006 1903(l) of the 21st Century Cures Act and any subsequent amendments, when applicable.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:_s256
Title: CAP IN-HOME AIDE II SERVICE
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched cover.
Content:
This is a service for a CAP/DA beneficiary who is unable to perform any two of the seven key Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) tasks independently due to a medical condition identified and documented on a validated assessment. This service provides limited to extensive hands-on assistance (not merely set-up or cueing) with or monitoring of at least two ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, hygiene, mobility and transferring). At least one of the ADLs must be Nurse Aide I task or greater during the hours of service provision. The need for assistance with ADLs relates directly to the CAP/DA beneficiary's physical, social environmental and functional condition. Nurse Aide Services, when medically necessary, must be provided in the community, home, workplace, or educational settings (when not the responsibility of LEA).
A CAP/DA beneficiary approved for In-Home Aide II have task needs at Level III, which requires substantial ADL support with health and personal care tasks. Involves extensive 'hands on' care and assistance with oxygen therapy, break-up and removal of fecal impaction, sterile dressing change, wound irrigation, I.V. fluid assistive activities, nutrition activities, suctioning, tracheostomy care, elimination procedures and urinary catheters. Level III tasks are considered higher-level tasks for CAP/DA. Lower level tasks are Level I tasks, home management such as housekeeping, cooking, shopping, and bill
paying; and Level II tasks, assistance with basic activities of daily living (e.g., eating, dressing, bathing, etc.) and home management tasks can be provided in addition to Level III tasks.
This service type is substantial. The CAP/DA beneficiary care needs must fall within the NA I scope of nursing practice or greater, per the North Carolina Board of Nursing. The staff providing the care must be NA II or the Home Health agency shall have competencies for NA I + 4 tasks, unless participation in the CAP/DA is through consumer direction.
Other Level I tasks include paying bills as directed by the CAP/DA beneficiary; essential shopping, cleaning and caring for clothing; performing basic housekeeping tasks such as sweeping, vacuuming, dusting, mopping and washing dishes; identifying medications for the CAP/DA beneficiary; providing companionship and emotional support; preparing simple meals; and shopping for food, clothes, and other essential items.
Nurse Aide services shall not be provided by personal care aides or home health aides not registered with DHSR, unless participation in the CAP/DA is through consumer direction.
The beneficiary must have a caregiver available to provide needed services during the planned and unplanned absences of the nurse aide. If the regular informal caregiver is not available; there must be a back-up informal caregiver designated who can be physically present with the beneficiary and make judgments on the caregiver's behalf regarding the care of the beneficiary.
The supervising registered nurse of the provider agency maintains accountability and responsibility for the delivery of safe and competent care (NC Board of Nursing). Decisions regarding the delegation of any nurse aide tasks are made by the licensed nurse on a beneficiary-by-beneficiary basis.
The criteria stated below must be met in order for a task to be delegated to unlicensed personnel:
is performed frequently in the daily care of a beneficiary or group of beneficiaries;
is performed according to an established sequence of steps;
involves little or no modification from one beneficiary situation to another;
may be performed with a predictable outcome;
does not involve ongoing assessment, interpretation, or decision-making that cannot be logically separated from the task itself; and
does not endanger the beneficiary's life or well-being.
Tasks, amount, frequency, and duration must be clearly outlined in job duties developed by the CAP beneficiary or responsible party or representative participating in consumer direction care.
Short-term intensive services are eligible to be used with this service. Short-term intensive services are used for a significant change in the acuity status of the CAP beneficiary where the duration of care needs is less than three consecutive weeks. Short-term intensive services are listed in the service plan. Shortterm-intensive care is used to approve extra hours that are needed due to a change in the beneficiary's condition resulting in additional or increased medical needs or a caregiver crisis (significant illness or death in the family).
Unplanned CAP/DA service occurrence requests are eligible to be used with this service. Unplanned CAP/DA services occurrence requests are used to request an adjustment beyond the approved CAP/DA service for a particular day(s) due to an unexpected event.
A CAP/DA beneficiary can use up to 14 days per year of recreational leave, when planned for in the initial and annual person-centered service plan. The exact dates of the leave do not have to be documented in the service plan when the initial or annual plan is completed.
Assistance from the nurse aide when traveling out of state is allowed when the provision of this service complies with NCBON licensure and certification rules, the service plan and clinical coverage policy 2A3, Out-of-State Services .
Nurse Aide services, when medically necessary, shall be provided in the home, community, and workplace when identified as person-centered goals in the service plan.
Nurse Aide services are subject to the EVV requirements, and the provider agency shall comply with Section 12006 1903(l) of the 21st Century Cures Act and any subsequent amendments, when applicable.
A paid live-in caregiver is excluded from the EVV requirements. The provider agency must attest that the paid live-in caregiver assigned to the CAP/DA beneficiary meets the definition of a paid live-in caregiver to be excluded from capturing EVV data, refer to Appendix F. Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Content:
The HCBS level of care targets an applicant and an active CAP/DA beneficiary who meets a nursing facility level of care (such as Medicaid Agency State Plan nursing facility level of care, 2B-1 Clinical Coverage Policy, with minor differences as described in the criteria below), due to a medical diagnosis or physical disability. Professional judgment and a thorough evaluation of the waiver participant's medical condition and psychosocial needs are required to differentiate between the need for nursing facility care and other health care alternatives. The HCBS LOC determination is based on the identification of conditions, diagnoses and treatments that are indicators of a care need that meets or exceeds the Medicaid State Plan nursing facility LOC criteria; and the presence of activities of daily living (ADLs) deficits that signal the need for the types of supplemental and supportive services this HCBS waiver can offer.
The HCBS LOC determination must address interventions, safeguards (health, safety and well-being) and the stability of each potential and actively approved CAP/DA beneficiary to ensure community integration and prevention of institutionalization because of chronic medical and physical disabilities.
A LOC determination must be completed at initial enrollment. An annual LOC is determined during the annual continued need review assessment. Changes to a beneficiary's condition that may cause the CAP/DA beneficiary to no longer meet HCBS LOC may result in disenrollment from waiver participation.

per_question.question: Under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, which DME items does NC Medicaid exclude from coverage, and what conditions have to be satisfied for an item to be covered at all?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid excludes certain orthotics/prosthetics-related devices and supplies from coverage under Policy 5B, and an item is covered only if the basic coverage conditions in the policy are met. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## What items are excluded from coverage?

Policy 5B says Medicaid does **not** cover these devices and supplies: devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver; devices kept as backup or duplicate devices for use in multiple locations; devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities; devices or supplies covered by another agency; and equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care. [Policy 5B § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy also says Medicaid does **not** cover a procedure, product, or service under this policy when the beneficiary does not meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0, does not meet the coverage criteria in Section 3.0, the item duplicates another provider’s procedure/product/service, or the item is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## What conditions have to be satisfied for any item to be covered?

For coverage at all, an orthotic or prosthetic device must be prescribed by the beneficiary’s treating physician, physician’s assistant, or nurse practitioner, and medical necessity must be documented. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Policy 5B defines medical necessity here as the device being needed to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy also indicates that listed items are identified through Attachment B and the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule, while items not listed there may still be considered for coverage if requested through a provider and submitted for prior authorization review of medical necessity. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Under-21 / EPSDT exception

For non-covered situations, Policy 5B specifically points readers to the EPSDT exception for Medicaid beneficiaries under age 21. [Policy 5B § 4.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

That EPSDT section says Medicaid must cover services, products, or procedures for beneficiaries under 21 if they are medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition identified through screening, and it says policy limits on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location, and other specific criteria may be exceeded or may not apply if the provider’s documentation shows the request meets EPSDT criteria. [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

I also checked amendments, and the knowledge base identifies Policy 5B itself as the current authoritative document. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

If you want, I can next pull together a **clean practitioner checklist** of the exact coverage prerequisites from Sections 2.0 and 3.0, since Section 4.1 makes those additional conditions part of the coverage test.

scores.explanation: The agent's answer accurately covers all key exclusions from sections 4.1 and 4.2.1 (comfort/convenience devices, backup/duplicate devices, nursing facility residents, items covered by another agency, hospice care, experimental items, duplicates of other providers' services, and failure to meet eligibility/coverage criteria). Coverage conditions from sections 1.0 and 3.2.1 are correctly described including physician/PA/NP prescription requirement and medical necessity documentation. The EPSDT exception for under-21 beneficiaries is properly noted. Citations are precise and section-level. Minor issue: the agent attributes some section 3.2.1 specific criteria (face-to-face encounter, annual review) to section 1.0 in one citation, which is a slight misattribution, but the content itself is accurate per the evidence. The agent also mentions 'face-to-face encounter' and 'annual review' requirements which appear in the golden dataset section 3.2.1 but not in the agent's retrieved evidence blocks - however these are in the curated golden-dataset sections provided in the evidence block, so they count as supported. Overall a thorough, well-cited, accurate response that a Medicaid policy expert would find acceptable.

Reason: Scope or description section for the yes/no coverage question.
Content:
Orthotic and prosthetic devices are covered by NC Medicaid (Medicaid) when they are prescribed by the beneficiary's treating physician, physician's assistant, or nurse practitioner and medical necessity is documented. An orthotic or prosthetic device is medically necessary if it is needed to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical, or functional level.
Covered orthotic and prosthetic devices become the property of the beneficiary.
Refer to Attachment B for a list of HCPCS codes, established lifetime expectancies, quantity limitations, and required provider certification for Orthotics and Prosthetics.
For the rates associated with the list of HCPCS codes found in Attachment B, refer to the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule at https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/providers.
In compliance with the CMS Home Health Final Rule Title 42, §440.70, items not listed in Attachment B or in the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule may be considered for coverage if requested by a provider, or a beneficiary through a provider, and submitted for prior authorization (PA) review of medical necessity. For beneficiaries under age 21, please request an 'EPSDT review' using NCTracks. Refer to section 2.2 Special Provisions for more information about EPSDT. For beneficiaries aged 21 and older, please submit the request through NCTracks per the procedure detailed in Attachment E: Requesting Unlisted Orthotics and Prosthetics for Adults .

Content:
Orthotic and prosthetic devices are covered by NC Medicaid (Medicaid) when they are prescribed by the beneficiary's treating physician, physician's assistant, or nurse practitioner and medical necessity is documented. An orthotic or prosthetic device is medically necessary if it is needed to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical, or functional level.
Covered orthotic and prosthetic devices become the property of the beneficiary.
Refer to Attachment B for a list of HCPCS codes, established lifetime expectancies, quantity limitations, and required provider certification for Orthotics and Prosthetics.
For the rates associated with the list of HCPCS codes found in Attachment B, refer to the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule at https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/providers.
In compliance with the CMS Home Health Final Rule Title 42, §440.70, items not listed in Attachment B or in the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule may be considered for coverage if requested by a provider, or a beneficiary through a provider, and submitted for prior authorization (PA) review of medical necessity. For beneficiaries under age 21, please request an 'EPSDT review' using NCTracks. Refer to section 2.2 Special Provisions for more information about EPSDT. For beneficiaries aged 21 and older, please submit the request through NCTracks per the procedure detailed in Attachment E: Requesting Unlisted Orthotics and Prosthetics for Adults .

Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

per_question.question: For outpatient behavioral health under NC Medicaid: what must be true for someone to start services, to keep receiving them, and to be discharged from them?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health, a person can **start services** only if they meet the policy’s entrance criteria, can **keep receiving services** only if they continue to meet the continued-service criteria, and can be **discharged** when any one of the discharge criteria is met. These rules appear in current Policy 8C, effective April 15, 2025, and the policy has been amended, including a 2025 revision removing prior-authorization language for telephonic services. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) [Policy 8C Change Notice 2025-04-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) [Policy 8C Change Notice 2025-01-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 1) What must be true to start services

To admit someone to outpatient treatment services, **all** of the following must be true: the person has a current DSM-5 diagnosis (or diagnosis under a subsequent edition), has behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment consistent with that diagnosis, is either appropriate for outpatient care or can receive outpatient care temporarily while a higher level of care is unavailable or refused, is capable of developing symptom-management and behavior-change skills and responding favorably to therapy, and there is no evidence that another intervention would be more effective under North Carolina community practice standards. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

For outpatient therapy services specifically, a licensed professional must complete a comprehensive clinical assessment (CCA) demonstrating medical necessity **before** the therapy begins, although the clinician may update a substantially equivalent recent assessment from another clinician if it reflects the beneficiary’s current functioning. [Policy 8C § 7.3.3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

That CCA must provide the clinical basis for the treatment or service plan and must be kept in the service record. [Policy 8C § 7.3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

The health record documentation for the assessment must include the presenting problem, the beneficiary’s needs and strengths, a provisional or admitting diagnosis with an established diagnosis within 30 calendar days, pertinent social, family, and medical history, and other evaluations or assessments as appropriate. [Policy 8C § 7.3.3.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

An individualized treatment or service plan is required within 15 business days of the first face-to-face beneficiary contact, must be based on the assessment, and must be developed in partnership with the beneficiary or legally responsible person. [Policy 8C § 7.3.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

NC Medicaid does **not** require prior approval for outpatient behavioral health services under this policy. [Policy 8C § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 2) What must be true to keep receiving services

To continue services, the person must meet **both** parts of the continued-service standard. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

First, **at least one** of these must be true: the desired outcome or level of functioning has not yet been restored, improved, or sustained within the timeframe in the treatment plan; the beneficiary remains at risk for relapse based on current clinical assessment and history; or the beneficiary’s functional gains are tenuous. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Second, **in addition**, **at least one** of these must be true: the beneficiary has achieved current treatment-plan goals but documented symptoms show that additional goals are indicated; or the beneficiary is making satisfactory progress toward goals and the documentation supports that continuing the service is expected to be effective in addressing the treatment-plan goals. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Ongoing services also have to remain tied to a current plan of care, because the plan must identify anticipated outcomes, strategies, responsible staff, review schedule, and the basis for evaluating outcomes, and updated or new plans must be signed by the beneficiary or legally responsible person and the licensed professional. [Policy 8C § 7.3.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Each treatment encounter must be supported by a progress note documenting the date, service, contact type, purpose tied to plan goals, interventions performed, effectiveness and response/progress, duration, and clinician signature/credentials, and the notes must show that interventions address the goals listed in the plan. [Policy 8C § 7.3.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Providers also must use a best practice or evidence-based treatment model expected to produce positive outcomes for the population treated and addressing the beneficiary’s clinical needs identified in the CCA and later assessments. [Policy 8C § 3.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 3) What must be true for discharge

A beneficiary may be discharged when **any one** of the following is true: the beneficiary’s level of functioning has improved with respect to the treatment-plan goals; the beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants the services; or the beneficiary has not improved despite treatment-plan modifications and, based on the presentation, needs a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 4) Important limits to remember

Outpatient behavioral health is not covered when the person has a medical, cognitive, intellectual, or developmental issue that would not benefit from outpatient treatment services, when the treatment focus does not address symptoms of the diagnosis, or when the policy’s requirements and limitations are not followed. [Policy 8C § 4.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Providers must also ensure access to 24-hour behavioral health crisis coverage, either directly or by written agreement with another entity, including the ability for the beneficiary to speak with the licensed clinician on call in person, by telehealth, or by telephone. [Policy 8C § 7.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

If helpful, I can turn this into a short **intake/continued-stay/discharge checklist** for advocates or providers.

scores.explanation: The agent's answer accurately captures all three phases from Policy 8C: entrance criteria (§3.2.1.1) with all five required conditions, continued service criteria (§3.2.1.2) with the two-part 'a and b' structure, and discharge criteria (§3.2.1.3) with the three alternative conditions. The answer goes well beyond the reference answer in useful detail, covering CCA requirements, treatment planning, progress notes, and exclusions - all supported by the evidence. Minor hallucination concern: the agent states the 2025-04-15 amendment date 'not changed' and references specific amendment language about telephonic services, which is supported in the evidence. The claim about 'sleep therapy for psychiatric disorders' in section 4.2.1.1 is supported in evidence. Citations are precise and section-level throughout. The answer is comprehensive and would be well-received by a Medicaid policy expert.

Medicaid shall not cover Outpatient Behavioral Health Services for the following:
sleep therapy for psychiatric disorders;
when services are not provided in-person or in accordance with Attachment A;
when a beneficiary presents with a medical, cognitive, intellectual or development issue that would not benefit from outpatient treatment services;
when the focus of treatment does not address the symptoms of the diagnosis;
when the requirements and limitations in Section 5.0 are not followed; and
when Psychotherapy for Crisis codes are billed, the same provider shall not bill Special Services: After Hours codes. Refer to clinical coverage policy 1A-38, Special Services: After Hours, located on NC Medicaid's website at https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/, for the same event.

Reason: Matched limitation.
Content:
Outpatient behavioral health service providers and those providing Psychotherapy for Crisis and psychological testing, shall be trained in and follow a rehabilitative best practice or evidence-based treatment model consistent with NC community practice standards. The treatment model must be expected to produce positive outcomes for the population being treated. The treatment model must address the clinical needs of the beneficiary identified in the comprehensive clinical assessment and on any subsequent assessments. Qualified interpreters shall be used, if necessary, to deliver test instructions in the examinee's preferred language.
Refer to Section 5.0 for additional requirements and limitations.

Title: C. Code(s)

Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched limitation.
Content:
Provider(s) shall report the most specific billing code that accurately and completely describes the procedure, product or service provided. Provider(s) shall use the Current Procedural Terminology (CPT), Health Care Procedure Coding System (HCPCS), ICD-10 procedure codes, and UB-04 Data Specifications Manual (for a complete listing of valid revenue codes) and any subsequent editions in effect at the time of service. Provider(s) shall refer to the applicable edition for the code description as it is no longer documented in the policy.
If no such specific CPT or HCPCS code exists, then the provider(s) shall report the procedure, product or service using the appropriate unlisted procedure or service code.
It is each billing provider's responsibility to read, understand, and ensure compliance with published CPT guidance and NC Medicaid policy for services billed to Medicaid and PIHP s. There is no substitute for reading the CPT manual. There are limitations to use of code combinations and documentation requirements listed in the manual that are not listed in this policy, but which providers must adhere to when billing Medicaid.
Physicians bill appropriate CPT codes which can contain Evaluation and Management (E/M) codes. E/M codes are not specific to mental health and are not subject to prior approval. These codes are subject to the annual visit limit for adults. For Medicaid beneficiaries under the age of 21 there is no limit to E/M codes allowed per state fiscal year.
Physicians billing E/M codes with psychotherapy add-on codes must have documentation supporting that the E/M service was separate and distinct from the psychotherapy service.
Documentation of E/M codes must follow the guidelines in the current version of the American Medical Association's Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codebook. Documentation must support the code billed and all of the components of the code selected must be documented.
Behavioral health-specific codes are billable by physicians according to the services they render and would be subject to prior approval if utilized. Other providers bill specific codes as indicated in the following CPT code table.
SBIRT services must only be billed when a clinician provides screening and brief intervention. If a brief intervention is not clinically indicated, time spent providing the screening must be incorporated in the time for other services rendered.

Medicaid shall cover outpatient behavioral health services when the beneficiary meets the following criteria:

[getSection]

Title: 3.2.1.1 Entrance Criteria
Section: 3.2.1.1
Policy: 8C
Type: clinical_policy

Citation link: [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Content:
All of the following criteria are necessary for admission of a beneficiary to outpatient treatment services:
A current Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition [(DSM-5) or any subsequent editions of this reference material] diagnosis;
The beneficiary presents behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment, which are consistent and associated with the current diagnosis;
If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable or the beneficiary is refusing the service, outpatient services can be provided until the appropriate level of care is available or to support the beneficiary to participate in that higher level of care;
The beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions;
There is no evidence to support that alternative interventions would be more effective, based on North Carolina community practice standards (Best Practice Guidelines of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, American Psychiatric Association, American Board of Addiction Medicine)

The criteria for continued service must meet both 'a.' and 'b.' below:
Any ONE of the following criteria:
The desired outcome or level of functioning has not been restored, improved, or sustained over the timeframe outlined in the beneficiary's treatment plan;
The beneficiary continues to be at risk for relapse based on current clinical assessment, and history: or
Tenuous nature of the functional gains.
Any ONE of the following criteria (in addition to 'a.')
The beneficiary has achieved current treatment plan goals, and additional goals are indicated as evidenced by documented symptoms; or
The beneficiary is making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals and there is documentation that supports that
continuation of this service is expected to be effective in addressing the goals outlined in the treatment plan.

Any ONE of the following criteria must be met:

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:8C:7.3.4
Title: 7.3.4 Individualized Plan
Section: 7.3.4
Policy: 8C
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2025-04-15
Citation link: [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Content:
An individualized plan of care, service plan, treatment plan, or PCP, referred to as 'plan,' consistent with and supportive of the service provided and within professional standards of practice, is required within 15 business days of the first face-to-face beneficiary contact. This plan is based on the assessment and is developed in partnership with the beneficiary or legally responsible person, or both. When services are provided prior to the establishment and implementation of the plan, strategies to address the beneficiary's presenting problem must be documented. The plan must be an identifiable document in the service record.
The plan must contain at a minimum:
beneficiary outcomes that are anticipated to be achieved by provision of the service and a projected date of achievement;
strategies;
staff responsible;
a schedule for review of the plan (in consultation with the beneficiary or legally responsible person or both) as needed but at least annually to review goals and strategies to promote effective treatment;
basis for evaluation or assessment of outcome achievement; and
written consent or agreement by the beneficiary or legally responsible person, or a written statement by the provider stating why such consent could not be obtained.
For a child or adolescent receiving outpatient substance use services, the plan must document both the staff and the child or adolescent's signatures demonstrating the involvement of all responsible parties in the development of the plan and the child or adolescent's consent or agreement to the plan. Consistent with N.C.G.S. § 90-21.5 or comparable federal, Tribal law, or rule, the plan may be implemented without parental consent when services are provided under the direction and supervision of a physician. When services are not provided under the direction and supervision of a physician, the plan must require the signature of the parent or legally responsible person for the child or adolescent demonstrating the involvement of the parent or legally responsible person in the development of the plan and the parent's or legally responsible person's consent to the plan.
The treatment plan must be updated as required, but a new plan is required at least annually.
All treatment plans must be developed in partnership with the beneficiary or legally responsible person, and all updated or new plans require the beneficiary or legally responsible person's signature, and the licensed professional's signature. The licensed professional's signature on the updated or new plan can serve as the service order.
Note: Beneficiaries receiving medication management only would be exempt from the requirement of having to sign the treatment plan. For beneficiaries receiving medication management only and who have a legally responsible person, the legally responsible person would also be exempt from this requirement. Refer to Attachment A, Section C for E/M code documentation requirements. The treatment plan for beneficiaries receiving only medication management would not need to be a separate document and could be integrated into service notes.

per_question.question: For a child under 21 receiving outpatient therapy, how does the EPSDT provision change what's covered, and who is permitted to order the therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
For a child under 21, EPSDT can expand outpatient therapy coverage beyond the usual policy limits when the therapy is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition identified through screening or evaluation. Under Policy 10A, that means limits on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria may be exceeded or may not apply if the provider documents that the requested therapy meets all EPSDT criteria. [Policy 10A § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) [Policy 10A § 3.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

For outpatient speech-language therapy specifically, Medicaid covers medically necessary treatment when prior authorization is received, and the under-21 section of the speech-language therapy criteria applies to children from birth through age 20. [Policy 10A § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

EPSDT does not remove prior authorization requirements. If the service requires prior approval, being under 21 does not eliminate that requirement. [Policy 10A § b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) Policy 10A also states that, for beneficiaries under 21, prior approval is required before the start of all treatment services, and the provider must submit information showing that all EPSDT criteria are met, along with supporting evidence-based literature if available. [Policy 10A § 5.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

So in practical terms, EPSDT can allow a child to receive medically necessary outpatient therapy even when ordinary policy visit or service limits would otherwise restrict coverage, but the provider still has to request and justify that expanded coverage through prior approval. [Policy 10A § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) [Policy 10A § 5.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

As to who may order the therapy, the outpatient specialized therapy service must be ordered by an NC Medicaid enrolled Medical Doctor, Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine, Doctor of Podiatric Medicine, Certified Nurse Midwife, Physician Assistant, or Nurse Practitioner. [Policy 10A § 3.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

The treatment plan itself is then developed after the evaluation and before treatment begins, in conjunction with the medical provider, the beneficiary, and for children, the parent or legal guardian. [Policy 10A § 3.2.1.6](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Policy 10A is current with an effective date of February 1, 2025, and the amendment lookup for that document did not identify a newer change notice replacing it. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also break this down by therapy type—PT, OT, speech, or audiology—or explain how EPSDT interacts with the visit ranges for children.

All claims are supported by the evidence blocks. Citations are precise and section-level. The answer is comprehensive, addressing both the EPSDT coverage expansion question and the ordering practitioner question fully. Section: 3.2.1.3

Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT or pediatric service section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover medically necessary outpatient speech-language therapy treatment for a beneficiary when prior authorization is received. Refer to Section 5.0.
Medically necessary treatment for oral phase, pharyngeal phase, or oropharyngeal phase dysphagia must contain documented findings.
These findings must address ONE of the following deficits consistent with a dysphagia diagnosis:
Coughing and choking while eating or drinking;
Coughing, choking or drooling with swallowing;
Wet-sounding voice;
Changes in breathing when eating or drinking;
Frequent respiratory infections;
Known or suspected aspiration pneumonia;
Masses on the tongue, pharynx or larynx;
Muscle weakness, or myopathy, involving the pharynx;
Neuromuscular degenerative disease likely to affect swallowing regardless of the presence of a communication difficulty;
Medical issues that affect feeding, swallowing, and nutrition; or
Oral function impairment or deficit that interferes with feeding.
These findings must be indicated through ONE of the following:
Video fluoroscopic swallowing exam (VFSE), also sometimes called a modified barium swallow exam (MBS);
Fiber optic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES); or,
Clinical feeding and swallowing evaluation.
For a beneficiary who is a minority language speaker, there is a continuum of proficiency in English.
Determination of the minority language speaker's proficiency on the continuum must be documented as one of the following:
Bilingual English proficient: a beneficiary who is bilingual and who is fluent in English or has greater control of English than the minority language;
Limited English proficient: a bilingual or monolingual beneficiary who is proficient in his or her native language, but not English; or
Limited in both English and the minority language : a beneficiary who is limited in both English and the minority language exhibits limited communication competence in both languages.
Evaluation must contain both objective and subjective measures to determine if the beneficiary is more proficient in either the English language or the minority language.
For speech and language therapy services to be medically necessary for a beneficiary who is a minority language speaker, ALL the following criteria must be met:
All speech deficits must be present in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest proficiency;
All language deficits must be present in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest proficiency;
The delivery of services must be in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest receptive language proficiency; and
If the use of interpreters or translators is the only alternative, the speech-language pathologist or audiologist must:
Provide sufficient instruction to the interpreter or translator regarding the purposes, procedures and goals of the tests and therapy methods;
For each date of service, the provider must ensure the interpreter or translator understands his or her role as it relates to the clinical procedures to be used and responses expected to address the goal;
Use the same interpreter or translator with a given beneficiary as consistently as possible; and
Use observation or other nonlinguistic measures as supplements to the translated measures, such as (1) beneficiary's interaction with parents, (2) beneficiary's interaction with peers, (3) pragmatic analysis.
The following criteria apply to a Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age:

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:2.2.1
Title: 2.2.1 EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age
Section: 2.2.1
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT or pediatric service section from the preferred document.
Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination ** (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed clinician).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:3.2.1.4
Title: 3.2.1.4 Audiology Therapy (Aural Rehabilitation)
Section: 3.2.1.4
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT or pediatric service section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover medically necessary audiology services when the beneficiary demonstrates the following:
the presence of any degree or type of hearing loss on the basis of the results of an audiologic (aural) rehabilitation evaluation; or
the presence of impaired or compromised auditory processing abilities based on the results of a central auditory test battery.
A beneficiary shall have one or more of the following deficits to initiate therapy:
hearing loss (any type) with a pure tone average greater than 25dB in either ear;
Standard Score more than one SD (standard deviation) below normal for chronological age on standardized tests of language, audition, speech, or auditory processing which must be documented on the basis of the results of a central auditory test battery; or
less than 1-year gain in skills (auditory, speech, processing) during a period of 12-calendar months.
Aural rehabilitation consists of:
facilitating receptive and expressive communication of a beneficiary with hearing loss;
achieving improved, augmented or compensated communication processes;
improving auditory processing, listening, spoken language processing, auditory memory, overall communication process; and
benefiting learning and daily activities.
Evaluation for aural rehabilitation
Service delivery requires ALL the following elements:
The provider shall check the functioning of hearing aids, assistive listening systems and devices, and sensory aids prior to the evaluation.
Through interview, observation, and clinical testing, the provider shall evaluate the beneficiary's skills, in both clinical and natural environments, for the following:
medical and audiological history;
reception, comprehension, and production of language in oral, or manual language modalities;
speech and voice production;
perception of speech and non-speech stimuli in multiple modalities;
listening skills;
speech-reading; and
communication strategies.
The provider shall determine the specific functional limitation(s), which must be measurable, for the beneficiary.
Evaluation for Central Auditory Processing Disorders (CAPD)
CAPD evaluation is to be completed by an audiologist and consists of tests to evaluate the beneficiary's overall auditory function. Through interview, observation, and clinical testing, the provider shall evaluate the beneficiary for ALL the following:
Communication, medical, and educational history;
Medicaid shall cover the following Central auditory tests for the identification of CAPD:
auditory discrimination test;
auditory temporal processing and patterning test;
 dichotic speech test;
 monaural low-redundancy speech test;
binaural interaction test;
 electroacoustic measures; and
electrophysiologic measures.
Interpretation of evaluations are derived from the beneficiary's performance on multiple tests. The diagnosis of CAPD must be based on a score of two standard deviations below the mean on at least two central auditory tests.
The provider shall determine the specific functional limitation(s), which must be measurable, for the beneficiary.
Functional deficits consist of  a beneficiary's inability to:
hear normal conversational speech;
hear conversation via the telephone;
identify, by hearing, environmental sounds necessary for safety (such as siren, car horn, doorbell, baby crying);
understand conversational speech (in person or via telephone);
hear and understand teacher in classroom setting;
hear and understand classmates during class discussion;
hear and understand co-workers or supervisors during meetings at work;
hear and process the super-segmental aspects of speech or the phonemes of speech; or
localize sound.
Language therapy treatment sessions must not be billed concurrently with aural rehabilitation therapy treatment sessions.
Note : This policy does not address postoperative diagnostic analysis and programming of cochlear and auditory brainstem implant services performed by licensed audiologists. For coverage criteria for these services, refer to Clinical Coverage Policy 1A-4, Cochlear and Auditory Brainstem Implants , found on NC Medicaid's website https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/

per_question.question: My mother lives in an adult care home (assisted living). Can she receive Personal Care Services through NC Medicaid while living there?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for someone living in an adult care home or assisted living–type setting, but only if she meets the congregate-setting PCS eligibility criteria in Policy 3L-1. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment) The policy says Medicaid covers PCS in a congregate facility licensed in North Carolina as an Adult Care Home or certain other qualifying group settings, and it also requires that the beneficiary meet functional and medical criteria. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

To qualify, your mother must have a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition that causes unmet needs with daily activities, and she must meet one of the policy’s ADL thresholds: at least three of five qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance, or two ADLs with one requiring extensive assistance, or two ADLs with one at the full-dependence level. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

The policy also requires, among other things, that the facility be a safe place for PCS to be delivered, that no other third-party payer be responsible for the service, that no available willing informal caregiver can provide the service during those times, that the need for PCS be directly linked to a documented condition or impairment, that she be under a physician’s ongoing direct care, and that she be medically stable and not require continuous licensed-nursing care, monitoring, or supervision. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

If she qualifies, covered PCS can include hands-on help with qualifying ADLs, related cueing or prompting when part of that hands-on help, certain IADL assistance tied to ADLs and essential to care at the residence, medication assistance tied to the condition, help with adaptive devices or durable medical equipment tied to ADLs, and certain delegated medical monitoring tasks. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

But Medicaid PCS in that setting does not cover room and board, transportation, errands, financial management, respite care, companion sitting or leisure activities, or skilled nursing services by an RN or LPN. [Policy 3L-1 § 4.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

The current policy document I relied on is marked amended January 1, 2026. [Policy 3L-1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

If you want, I can next help with either:
- a quick checklist to see whether she likely meets the PCS criteria, or
- what to do if the adult care home says Medicaid will not pay for PCS there.

scores.explanation: The agent's answer is fully accurate, citing Policy 3L-1 sections 3.2.1, 3.3, and 4.2.1.2 precisely. It correctly identifies that congregate PCS is governed by Policy 3L-1 (not the in-home 3L policy), accurately describes the ADL thresholds, facility requirements, additional eligibility criteria, covered services, and non-covered services. All claims are directly supported by the Evidence block. The answer also notes the January 1, 2026 amendment date, which appears in the evidence. No hallucinations detected. The response is thorough, well-organized, and would be accepted by a Medicaid policy expert.

Title: 3.2.1 Specific criteria covered by Medicaid
Section: 3.2.1
Policy: 3L-1
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)
Reason: Congregate PCS beneficiary and facility criteria section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings when the beneficiary meets the following specific criteria and other items in this section:
has a medical or mental condition, disability, or cognitive impairment and demonstrates unmet needs for, at a minimum:
three of the five qualifying activities of daily living (ADLs) with limited hands-on assistance. Refer to Subsection 5.4.3;
two ADLs, one of which requires extensive assistance; or
two ADLs, one of which requires assistance at the full dependence level.
resides in:
a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH) as defined in NC G.S. §131D-2.1, a combination home as defined in NC G.S. § 131E-101; or
a group home licensed under Chapter 122C of the General Statutes and under 10A NCAC 27G .5601 (b)(2) as a supervised living facility for two or more adults whose primary diagnosis is mental illness, a developmental disability, or substance abuse dependency and is eligible to receive personal care services under the Medicaid State Plan.
In addition to the specific criteria in Subsection 3.2.1 a and b of this policy, the following criteria must be met:
The congregate setting is safe and free of health hazards for the beneficiary and PCS provider(s), as determined by a facility environmental assessment conducted by NC Medicaid or a DHHS designated contractor;
The congregate setting has received inspection conducted by the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR)
The place of service is safe for the beneficiary to receive PCS and for an aide to provide PCS;
No other third-party payer is responsible for covering PCS;
No family or household member or other informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services during those periods of time when the services are provided;
The required PCS are directly linked to a documented medical or mental condition or physical or cognitive impairment causing the functional limitations requiring the PCS;
The beneficiary is under the ongoing direct care of a physician for the medical condition or diagnosis causing the functional limitations; and
The beneficiary is medically stable and does not require continuous care, monitoring (precautionary observation), or supervision (observation resulting in an intervention) by a licensed nurse or other licensed health care professional; and
Screening for Serious Mental Illness (SMI) in Adult Care Homes licensed under G.S. §131D-2.4 Effective November 1, 2018, any Medicaid beneficiary referred to or seeking admission to Adult Care Homes licensed under G.S. 131D-2.4 must be referred to a Tailored Plan Transition Coordinator for the Referral Screening Verification Process. Adult Care Home providers licensed under G.S. § 131D-2.4 shall not receive a PCS assessment or prior approval without verification of a Referral Screening ID.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3L-1:3.3
Title: 3.3 Personal Care Services
Section: 3.3
Policy: 3L-1
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)
Reason: Congregate PCS covered-service section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover the following Personal Care Services that occur at minimum, once per week:
Hands-on assistance to address unmet needs with qualifying ADLs;
Set-up, supervision, cueing, prompting, and guiding, when provided as part of the hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs;
Assistance with home management Instrumentals of Daily Living (IADLs) that are directly related to the beneficiary's qualifying ADLs and essential to the beneficiary's care at their private residence;
Assistance with medication when directly linked to a documented medical condition or physical or cognitive impairment as specified in Subsection 3.2 ;
Assistance with adaptive or assistive devices when directly linked to the qualifying ADLs;
Assistance with the use of durable medical equipment when directly linked to the qualifying ADLs; or
Assistance with special assistance (assistance with ADLs that requires a Nurse aide II) and delegated medical monitoring tasks.

Skilled nursing services provided by a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) or Registered Nurse (RN);

Transportation;
Financial management;
Errands;

Title: 7.3.2 Home Health Services
Section: 7.3.2
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
Reason: Direct coverage-detail section from the preferred document.
Content:
Because home health agencies can also provide supplies, the provider shall coordinate the provision of orthotic and prosthetic devices and related supplies with any home health agency serving a Medicaid beneficiary to ensure that supplies being provided by the home health agency are not being duplicated.
If orthotic or prosthetic devices are being provided to a home health beneficiary, the home health agency staff may be involved in helping the Medicaid beneficiary learn how to use the equipment and may be monitoring its use. The provider shall ensure that the beneficiary and caregiver:
Know how to care for the orthotic and prosthetic devices and related supplies; and
Understand the rights and responsibilities of the beneficiary, the caregiver, and the provider agency.
Note: The provider shall give the beneficiary and caregiver written instructions that contain emergency provisions and a telephone number for contacting the provider agency 24 hours per day.

Section: 3.2

Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
Reason: Direct coverage-detail section from the preferred document.
Content:
[Container heading with 2 child sections:]

### 3.2.2 Medicaid Additional Criteria Covered
None Apply.

### 3.2.1 Specific criteria covered by Medicaid
Medicaid shall cover orthotics and prosthetics when the beneficiary meets all the following specific criteria:
they are ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner;
they are medically necessary to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical or functional level, and appropriate for use in any noninstitutional setting in which normal life activities take place;
a documented face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary and the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner related to the primary reason the beneficiary requires orthotics and prosthetics has occurred no more than six (6) months prior to the initiation of orthotics and prosthetics; and
the beneficiary's need for orthotics and prosthetics is reviewed by the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner at least annually.
Medicaid covers orthotic and prosthetic services when they are medically necessary, and the beneficiary meets the specific coverage requirements for the device.
Orthotic devices are medically necessary when required to correct or prevent skeletal deformities, to support or align movable body parts, or to preserve or improve physical function.
Prosthetic devices are medically necessary as a replacement for all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part. The beneficiary shall require the prosthesis for mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes.
In addition, orthotic and prosthetic devices must be:
a reasonable and medically necessary part of the beneficiary's treatment plan;
consistent with the beneficiary's diagnosis and medical condition, particularly the functional limitations and symptoms exhibited by the beneficiary; and
of high quality, with replacement parts available and obtainable.
Medical doctors (MDs), doctors of osteopathic medicine (DOs), doctors of podiatric medicine (DPMs), physician assistants (PAs) and nurse practitioners (NPs) may provide certain orthotic and prosthetic devices when the devices are part of the beneficiary's current care and treatment. These professionals may provide devices as indicated in the Required Provider Certification column of Attachment B .
To be reimbursed for an orthotic or prosthetic device, the provider shall be enrolled as an appropriate board-certified provider for the specific device. Refer to Attachment B, which includes the Required Professional Certification for Orthotic and Prosthetic Devices.
For specific coverage requirements, refer to Subsection 5.3, Documenting Medical Necessity.



ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:5B:2.2.1
Title: 2.2.1 EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age
Section: 2.2.1
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT special-provision section that may modify policy limitations for beneficiaries under 21.
Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed practitioner).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

Content:
[Container heading with 2 child sections:]

### 3.2.2 Medicaid Additional Criteria Covered
None Apply.

### 3.2.1 Specific criteria covered by Medicaid
Medicaid shall cover orthotics and prosthetics when the beneficiary meets all the following specific criteria:
they are ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner;
they are medically necessary to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical or functional level, and appropriate for use in any noninstitutional setting in which normal life activities take place;
a documented face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary and the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner related to the primary reason the beneficiary requires orthotics and prosthetics has occurred no more than six (6) months prior to the initiation of orthotics and prosthetics; and
the beneficiary's need for orthotics and prosthetics is reviewed by the ordering physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner at least annually.
Medicaid covers orthotic and prosthetic services when they are medically necessary, and the beneficiary meets the specific coverage requirements for the device.
Orthotic devices are medically necessary when required to correct or prevent skeletal deformities, to support or align movable body parts, or to preserve or improve physical function.
Prosthetic devices are medically necessary as a replacement for all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part. The beneficiary shall require the prosthesis for mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes.
In addition, orthotic and prosthetic devices must be:
a reasonable and medically necessary part of the beneficiary's treatment plan;
consistent with the beneficiary's diagnosis and medical condition, particularly the functional limitations and symptoms exhibited by the beneficiary; and
of high quality, with replacement parts available and obtainable.
Medical doctors (MDs), doctors of osteopathic medicine (DOs), doctors of podiatric medicine (DPMs), physician assistants (PAs) and nurse practitioners (NPs) may provide certain orthotic and prosthetic devices when the devices are part of the beneficiary's current care and treatment. These professionals may provide devices as indicated in the Required Provider Certification column of Attachment B .
To be reimbursed for an orthotic or prosthetic device, the provider shall be enrolled as an appropriate board-certified provider for the specific device. Refer to Attachment B, which includes the Required Professional Certification for Orthotic and Prosthetic Devices.
For specific coverage requirements, refer to Subsection 5.3, Documenting Medical Necessity.
